title: Do this week
note: Eleven jobs across five areas. Two of them have a window that closes; the rest buy you flowers or head off a problem, and nothing dies if they slip.

tasks.title: Shake the poppy seed where you want it
body: Those hundreds of little pods are ripe or nearly ripe, and once they shatter the seed goes wherever it goes. Hold each stem over the spot you want poppies next spring and tip the pod. It pours out like a pepper shaker.
Shirley poppies will not transplant and resent spring sowing, so this fall drop is your only real shot at next year's display. Put a pinch in an envelope as insurance before you scatter the rest.
tasks.ifSkipped: The pods shatter and next spring's poppies come up wherever they happen to land, not where you want them.

tasks.title: Deadhead the gaillardia hard, then the dahlias
body: Across the photos there are roughly two dozen spent seed globes for every open gaillardia flower. Once the plant decides it has made enough seed, it quits blooming. Cut each spent globe back to a leaf or side shoot, not just the ball off the top.

Same move on the dahlias: cut back to a set of leaves or a stem junction. Buds are round and firm, spent heads are pointed and conical. Then the scabiosa. Done properly this is worth six to eight more weeks of flowers.
tasks.ifSkipped: Nothing dies. The plants set seed and stop flowering several weeks earlier than they would have.

tasks.title: Quick thrips check on the gladiolus
body: These corms already overwinter in the beds and come back, so the baseline is good and the yellowing is most likely ordinary post-bloom senescence. This check only rules out the one thing that would change the routine.

Hold white paper under a leaf and flick the leaf sharply. Thrips look like tiny dark slivers moving fast on the paper. The proper inspection happens in fall anyway, when the corms are out of the ground.
tasks.ifSkipped: You find out anyway when the corms come out of the ground in fall.

tasks.title: Inspect the split stem
body: Closed. A thick green stalk appeared to have a long vertical crack in one photo, but nothing obvious in the bed, so it was almost certainly minor growth cracking that has already healed over.
tasks.ifSkipped: Closed, nothing to skip.

tasks.title: Cut the spent gladiolus spikes, keep the leaves
body: The green seed capsules swelling on those spikes are pulling energy the corm needs to size up for next year. Cut the flower spike at its base. Leave every leaf until it yellows completely.
tasks.ifSkipped: Smaller corms and weaker flowers next summer.

tasks.title: Strip the mildewed sunflower leaves
body: The white powdery coating on the side bed sunflowers is powdery mildew. It is not worth spraying this late on plants that are nearly finished. Pull off the worst leaves, especially the low ones, and bin them rather than putting them in the tumbler.

The cause is the spot, not the plant. A west wall gives shade all morning, then hard afternoon heat radiating off the wall, over roots kept dry by the foundation and the eave. Warm, still and dry-rooted is what powdery mildew wants. Sunflowers want open sun and steady moisture, so move them to the street boxes next year.
tasks.ifSkipped: Cosmetic on plants that are nearly finished. It looks bad and does almost nothing.

tasks.title: Weed the strawberry mat before anything seeds
body: There is a low creeping ground cover running between the strawberry crowns, plus a few broadleaf rosettes. Get them out now while the soil is soft and before they set seed.

Identify the creeper before you assume it is harmless. Chickweed pulls out in soft mats and is a minor annual nuisance. Ground ivy roots at every node and is a multi-year problem, and telling them apart takes ten seconds.
tasks.ifSkipped: They seed, and next spring's weeding takes several times as long.

tasks.title: Check how dry the soil is against the foundation
body: Push a finger in to the second knuckle right up against the wall, then again at the front edge of the bed. The strip beside a house is usually the driest soil in a garden: the wall throws a rain shadow, the foundation wicks moisture away, and any eave overhead keeps rain off entirely.
If the back is noticeably drier than the front, that explains the stressed sunflowers, and the fix is simply watering that strip separately rather than assuming the whole bed gets the same.
tasks.ifSkipped: You keep watering the whole bed the same and the back stays thirsty.

tasks.title: Cut back the spent shasta daisies
body: Confirmed as shasta daisy. Almost every flower on that stand is finished, and the bed is reading as brown from the sidewalk because of it. Cut the spent stems down to the low mound of fresh green leaves at the base, which stays through winter.
Leave a few seedheads standing if you want it to self-sow, but only a few. This one seeds itself generously.
tasks.ifSkipped: It looks brown from the sidewalk. The plant is completely fine.

tasks.title: Deal with the volunteer seedling
body: There is a woody seedling with divided leaves coming up through the back of the bed. Ash and elder both self-sow all over Seattle and both become trees.
Photograph a whole leaf laid flat and note whether leaves come off the stem in opposite pairs, then pull it. It will never be easier to remove than it is right now.
tasks.ifSkipped: It gets meaningfully harder to remove every year, and eventually needs a saw.

tasks.title: Confirm the orientation
body: Closed. Confirmed three ways: the street is the north side, south is where the townhomes are, and the Side Bed Box is on the west wall. All three agree on a standard north-up plan, which also matches your original hand sketch and your observation that the street boxes are full sun.
Every area's aspect now derives from that one fact rather than being guessed bed by bed.
tasks.ifSkipped: Closed.

tasks.title: Deadhead the zinnias, deep
body: Zinnias are cut-and-come-again, and they reward hard cutting. Do not snip the flower off the top: follow the stem down to where it meets a pair of leaves or a side shoot and cut there. You get two new flowering stems from every cut.
Leave three or four of the best heads uncut to dry on the plant for seed. Zinnia seed is among the easiest to save and it is worth having.
tasks.ifSkipped: Flowering tails off within a few weeks instead of running to frost.

tasks.title: Read the light off the plants themselves
body: Sunflowers and zinnias make good light meters, so this bed can confirm its own sun without you timing shadows. Stout upright sunflower stems with big heads mean full sun. Thin stems leaning hard in one direction with small heads mean they are reaching for light they are not getting.
Same story for the zinnias: compact and smothered in flowers is full sun, tall and floppy with few flowers is not enough. Tell me which you see and I will fix the map.
tasks.ifSkipped: The map keeps a guess in it where it could have a fact.

title: The sowing window
note: The highest-leverage three weeks of the gardening year, and almost nobody uses them. Hardy annuals sown now germinate in warm soil, overwinter as small plants, and bloom in May and June, months earlier and twice the size of anything spring-sown.

tasks.title: Direct-sow hardy annuals into the gaps
body: Street Bed 2 is the sowing bed, because pulling the spent poppies opens real ground. Larkspur, nigella, bachelor's button, breadseed poppy, calendula, orlaya. Scatter, press in, do not bury deep, keep damp until the rains take over.
tasks.ifSkipped: Sow in spring instead and you get later, smaller, shorter-lived plants. The fall window does not come back.

tasks.title: Clear the spent poppies and dead material
body: After the seed is shaken, pull the poppy plants. They are annuals and they are finished.

Leave the snapdragons. Cut their spent spikes off but keep the plants: they are hardy enough to overwinter here and often come back for a second year. Let two or three spikes stand and shatter if you want them to self-sow.
Before pulling the big silver-grey mass, squeeze a stem near the base. Brittle and hollow means dead, pull it. Still flexible and green inside means alive and just ugly, leave it.
tasks.ifSkipped: It looks untidy over winter. Some gardeners prefer it that way.

tasks.title: Shear the oregano by a third, dry the leaves
body: It has already flowered so the leaves are past peak flavour, but they are still worth drying. Cutting now stops it going leggy and woody in the middle. Stay out of the old wood: save hard renewal pruning for spring.
tasks.ifSkipped: It gets leggier and woodier, and you fix it in spring instead.

tasks.title: Shear the hardy geranium back hard
body: Cut the cranesbill to a few inches. It looks brutal and it works: a fresh low mound of clean foliage within two or three weeks, and often a second flush of flowers before frost.
tasks.ifSkipped: You miss a second flush of flowers and some fresh foliage. That is all.

tasks.title: Thin the strawberry mat and take runner cuttings
body: These are flowering and fruiting at the end of August, which makes them everbearing or day-neutral rather than June-bearing. That matters: do not mow the foliage down. The renovation advice you will find everywhere online is for June-bearing types and would cost you fruit.

What they do need is space. The mat is crowded, and crowded strawberries give small fruit and hold damp air around the crowns. Thin to roughly one plant every six to eight inches, taking out the oldest woodiest crowns first. Plants decline after three or four years, so peg down a few runners into the gaps to root as free replacements and cut the rest off.
tasks.ifSkipped: Smaller fruit and crowded damp crowns next season, and the decline compounds.

tasks.title: Keep picking the beans, then cut at soil level
body: Picking is what keeps them producing. Every pod left to mature tells the plant it is done. You have roughly four to six weeks left.
When they finish, cut the stems at soil level rather than pulling them up. The roots carry nitrogen-fixing nodules, and leaving them in place feeds whatever goes in that spot next year.
tasks.ifSkipped: Picking is what keeps them producing, so they stop early.

tasks.title: Divide the bearded iris
body: Confirmed as bearded iris, so this is worth doing properly. The window is roughly six weeks after flowering through early September, and you are at the end of it.

Lift the clump, snap the rhizomes apart so each piece has a fan of leaves and some roots, and throw away anything soft, hollow or smelly. Cut the leaves back to a fan about six inches tall so wind cannot rock the new divisions loose.

Replant shallow, with the top of each rhizome visible above the soil. Iris planted too deep is the single most common reason it stops flowering, and burying a rhizome in wet Seattle soil is how it rots.
tasks.ifSkipped: The window is gone until next August, and a congested clump flowers less every year in the meantime.

tasks.title: Peg down the sprawling rosemary branches
body: The rosemary has opened up and thrown long bare branches flat across the soil. Rather than cutting them off, pin a few down where they touch the ground with a rock or a bent wire. They root along the buried section over winter, and you can cut them free as new plants in spring.
This is also the fix for the bare woody centre. You cannot prune rosemary back into old wood to rejuvenate it, so growing replacements is the way to renew the planting.
tasks.ifSkipped: You lose a free year of replacement plants, and the bare centre stays bare.

tasks.title: Survey the remaining five areas
body: Five of eleven areas have not been looked at. Back Bed 1 in the south-east corner is the only remaining candidate for real sun, since it sits clear of the house on the south side.
Photograph each and note what is already growing there. Sun aside, there may be more usable growing space here than anyone has counted.
tasks.ifSkipped: The plan stays partly blank. No plant suffers.

tasks.title: Stop all fertilizing
body: Soft new growth heading into a wet Seattle autumn is asking for rot and mildew. Nothing more goes on the beds until spring.
tasks.ifSkipped: Soft new growth going into the wet, which invites rot and mildew.

tasks.title: Keep watering deeply, once a week
body: September here looks wet and usually is not. A street-side raised box in full sun dries fast, and dahlias stop setting buds the moment they go dry. Carry on until real rain arrives, roughly mid-October.
tasks.ifSkipped: Dahlias stop setting buds the moment they run dry, and do not restart quickly.

tasks.title: Buy spring bulbs now, plant them later
body: Selection is best in September and planting is October and November. Both beds have room once the annuals come out.
tasks.ifSkipped: The good selection is gone by late October. You can still plant, with less choice.

title: October
note: The month the weather turns. The enemy from here is not cold, it is botrytis: grey mould on dense flower heads once the rain sets in.

tasks.title: Switch to mould patrol
body: Pull spent petals off the plant rather than letting them rot in place, especially on the dahlias. Thin enough stems that air moves through the bed. This one habit prevents most of the damage.
tasks.ifSkipped: Grey mould spreads through dense flower heads once the rain sets in.

tasks.title: Sow sweet peas, start planting bulbs
body: Sweet peas go in around mid-October for the earliest and strongest spring plants.

Bulbs matter more here than I realised. The front beds are a tulip display, and tulips fade after a year or two in wet Pacific Northwest soil, so the show is maintained by topping up rather than by the same bulbs returning. Daffodils do come back and multiply, so those are worth adding for the part of the display that looks after itself.
tasks.ifSkipped: Fall-sown sweet peas are the strong ones. Spring sowing gives noticeably weaker plants.

tasks.title: Cut the gladiolus foliage once it is fully yellow
body: Not before. Green leaves are still feeding the corm. When they have gone completely yellow, cut them at ground level.
tasks.ifSkipped: Untidy over winter, and no harm at all as long as you do not cut it while still green.

tasks.title: Top-dress with compost
body: An inch or two over the soil surface, not piled against any crowns. Winter rain works it in for you.
tasks.ifSkipped: Soil improves more slowly. Nothing is damaged.

tasks.title: Keep the fall tidy away from the rosemary and sage
body: This is the one to remember when the urge to cut everything down arrives. Pruning woody Mediterranean herbs in fall pushes out soft growth that then dies in the first cold snap, and cutting into their bare wood leaves a permanent hole because neither one resprouts from it.
Leave both untouched until spring. Keep compost and mulch off their crowns too: they die of wet feet here far more often than of cold.
tasks.ifSkipped: Cut a woody Mediterranean herb into bare wood and the hole is permanent. This one is not recoverable.

tasks.title: Collect the zinnia seed
body: Take the heads you left standing once they are brown and crisp, not before. Damp seed rots in storage. Pull the dried head apart and the seeds are the arrowhead-shaped flakes at the base of each petal.
Dry them another week indoors on a plate, then into a paper envelope somewhere cool. Zinnias resent transplanting, so sow them straight into the ground after the last frost next spring.
tasks.ifSkipped: The heads rot or shatter over winter and the seed is gone.

tasks.title: Top up the tulips in the front beds
tasks.ifSkipped: Next spring's display is thinner than this one, and thinner again the year after. Nothing dies, it just quietly fades.
body: This is the one bit of real upkeep the front beds need, and it is once a year. Plant fresh bulbs into the gaps in October or November, deep, about three times the height of the bulb.

If you want to shrink even this job, lean toward the kinds that persist here: Darwin hybrids and species tulips come back far better than the big fancy ones, and daffodils return and multiply on their own indefinitely.

title: After first frost
note: In-city Seattle often does not freeze until mid-November, occasionally not until December. Do not act on the calendar, act on the first night that actually blackens the dahlia foliage.

tasks.title: Put the dahlias to bed
body: Cut the blackened stalks to about four inches. Cap the hollow stems so winter rain cannot funnel down into the crown, then cover with a few inches of coarse mulch.
In a raised box that drains well, leaving tubers in the ground is a reasonable bet here. The risk is rot in saturated soil, not freezing. Dig and store only for zero risk.
tasks.ifSkipped: Water funnels into the open stems and the tubers rot over winter. This is the difference between having dahlias next year and not.

tasks.title: Lift, inspect and spread the gladiolus corms
body: This is the job already done here each fall. The only addition is looking at each corm as it comes up. Firm and smooth is healthy. Rough corky brown patches, sometimes with a sticky varnished sheen, means thrips. Anything rough or shrivelled goes in the trash, not back in the bed and not in the compost.

Each season the old corm is used up and a new one forms on top, usually with a cluster of tiny cormels around the base. Those cormels are free plants. Pick them off and grow them on in a nursery corner rather than letting them crowd the parents, and they reach flowering size in two or three years.
tasks.ifSkipped: The clump gets congested and any thrips carry through to next summer.

tasks.title: Leave more standing than feels tidy
body: Leave the echinacea seedheads for goldfinches and the sunflower heads for everything else. Cut the gaillardia to four to six inches rather than to the ground, so water cannot sit in a hollow crown, and keep mulch off its centre. Gaillardia dies of wet feet here, never of cold.
tasks.ifSkipped: You lose the bird food and the frost interest. The plants do not mind.

callout.title: And then the front beds do the work
callout.body: Spring is when the standing seedheads come down, the oregano gets hard-pruned into old wood, and the mulch comes off the dahlia crowns. It is also when the front beds pay out, with no input from you beyond having planted the bulbs. Leave every bulb leaf until it has yellowed completely: that is when next year's flower gets made.
